overview:
Kayotsarga (Sanskrit: "kāyotsarga", Jain Prakrit: "kāussagga") is a central Jain meditative posture and spiritual discipline whose literal meaning is "abandonment" or "dismissal of the body" (kāya = body, utsarga = giving up). In classical Jain usage it does not imply hatred of the body, but the deliberate loosening of attachment to the physical personality so that attention can be absorbed in the true nature of the soul (jīva). The practitioner remains motionless—most characteristically in a standing posture, though sitting and other stable postures are also attested—while cultivating equanimity, repentance, and contemplation of the self as distinct from the body.

In the normative ascetic framework, kayotsarga is counted among the six essential duties (āvaśyaka) of a Jain monk or nun and is also integrated into the daily observances of lay followers through rites such as pratikramaṇa and sāmāyika. During these rites, kayotsarga functions as a phase of withdrawal of attention from bodily movements and comforts, following confession of faults and vows of restraint. It is closely linked with the purification of karmic "wounds" or defects (ātiśaya/atichāra) that obscure right knowledge (jñāna), right perception (darśana), and right conduct (cāritra). Texts describe kayotsarga as a means of prāyaścitta (penance), viśodhikaraṇa (special purification), and viśallikaraṇa (removal of the "thorns" of deceit, craving, and wrong belief.

Historically, the conceptual root of kayotsarga appears in early canonical passages that speak of "giving up the body" or "one who has abandoned the body" as a defining trait of the true ascetic. Later ritual manuals such as the Āvaśyaka-sūtra systematize kayotsarga into a prescribed sequence of posture, recitation, and mental focus, making it part of the twice-daily obligatory rites for monastics and, in adapted form, for laypeople. In iconography, tirthankaras are represented either seated in meditation or standing in kayotsarga, and Jain tradition holds that many tirthankaras—including Bahubali—attained liberation while maintaining this unflinching standing meditation.

From the perspective of lay practice, kayotsarga is also associated with graded stages of spiritual progress (pratimā). Some medieval authors use the term kāyotsargapratimā for a stage characterized by intensified continence, night-long meditation in kayotsarga on fast days, and renunciation of certain bodily indulgences such as eating after sunset. In modern Jain discourse, kayotsarga continues to be interpreted both ritually and meditatively: traditional commentaries emphasize its role in karmic shedding and ethical purification, while contemporary meditation movements sometimes present it as a technique of relaxation and body-detachment grounded in ancient ascetic discipline. Across these interpretations, the core remains the same: a disciplined stillness of the body that supports inner transformation, repentance, and realization of the soul’s independence from the physical frame.

primary_sources.title: Ācārāṅga-sūtra
primary_sources.author: Traditionally attributed to Mahāvīra’s disciples; canonical Śvetāmbara text
primary_sources.original_text:
कयं वोसज्जमङ्गारे
वोसट्ठकाए समणे त्ति वच्चे
primary_sources.transliteration:
kayaṃ vosajjamaṅgāre
vosaṭṭhakāe samaṇe tti vacce
primary_sources.translation:
“An ascetic is one who has given up the body in the glowing embers.
One who abandons the body is called an ascetic.”
primary_sources.notes: These early canonical passages, cited together with parallel lines in the Sūtrakṛtāṅga-sūtra, express the ideal of "giving up the body" as a hallmark of true renunciation. While the specific term "kayotsarga" is not yet used, later tradition reads these descriptions of abandoning attachment to the body as the conceptual foundation of kayotsarga practice, where the ascetic stands or sits motionless, relinquishing bodily concerns to focus on the soul.

primary_sources.title: Āvaśyaka-sūtra
primary_sources.author: Canonical Śvetāmbara ritual manual; author not individually named
primary_sources.original_text:
इच्छामि ठामि काउस्सग्गं
तस्स उत्तरिकरणेण, पयच्छित्तकरणेण, विसोधिकरणेण, विसल्लिकरणेण, पापाणं कर्माणं निद्घाटनाथाए ठामि काउस्सग्गं… तावकारियं ठाणेण मोणेण झाणेण अप्पाणं वोसिरामि।
primary_sources.transliteration:
ichchāmi ṭhāmi kāussaggaṃ
tassa uttarikaraṇeṇa, payacchittkaraṇeṇa, visodhikaraṇeṇa, visallikaraṇeṇa, pāpāṇaṃ karmāṇaṃ nidghāṭanāthāe ṭhāmi kāussaggaṃ… tāvakāryaṃ ṭhāṇeṇa moṇeṇa jhāṇeṇa āppāṇaṃ vosirāmi.
primary_sources.translation:
“I desire to stand in kayotsarga.
For the sake of excellence, for penance, for special purification, for the removal of thorns, and for the destruction of sinful karmas, I stand in kayotsarga… For this purpose, by standing, by silence, by meditation, I cause my own self to be well-established.”
primary_sources.notes: The Āvaśyaka-sūtra gives one of the earliest formulaic descriptions of kayotsarga as part of the daily obligatory rites (āvaśyaka). The practitioner explicitly states the intention behind kayotsarga: excellence of the soul, penance, purification, removal of spiritual "thorns", and destruction of sinful karmas. Commentarial traditions elaborate the posture (usually standing with feet slightly apart, arms relaxed) and the mental focus on repentance and detachment from the body.

primary_sources.title: Uttarādhyayana-sūtra
primary_sources.author: Canonical Śvetāmbara text; traditionally linked to early Jain community
primary_sources.translation: “By kayotsarga there is purification; and purification indeed belongs to the meritorious.”
primary_sources.notes: This line, cited in later discussions of kayotsarga, connects the practice directly with purification (viśuddhi) and merit (puṇya). In the broader context of the Uttarādhyayana-sūtra, kayotsarga is treated as a disciplined posture and mental state that supports repentance, confession of faults, and the cultivation of equanimity. Traditional commentaries use such verses to argue that kayotsarga is not merely physical stillness but a moral and spiritual act aimed at cleansing karmic impurities.

primary_sources.title: Anuyogadvāra-sūtra
primary_sources.author: Canonical Śvetāmbara text on hermeneutics and practice
primary_sources.translation: “Kayotsarga is like the cleansing of a wound.”
primary_sources.notes: The Anuyogadvāra-sūtra uses the metaphor of wound-cleansing to describe kayotsarga. The "wounds" are the injuries to the soul caused by passions, attachments, and transgressions that damage knowledge, perception, and conduct. Kayotsarga, performed with repentance and detachment, is likened to the careful cleaning of these wounds so that healing can occur. Later authors build on this image to explain kayotsarga as a therapeutic spiritual practice that restores the soul’s inherent purity.

misconceptions.myth: Kayotsarga is only a rigid standing posture and cannot be performed in any other position.
misconceptions.reality: Classical descriptions emphasize standing kayotsarga as the iconic posture, especially in the depiction of tirthankaras and in accounts of Bahubali’s year-long meditation. However, ritual manuals and commentaries also acknowledge kayotsarga in other stable postures, including sitting, as long as the essential element—withdrawal of attention from bodily movements and cultivation of detachment—is maintained. The defining feature is inner non-attachment and stillness, not a single externally fixed pose.

misconceptions.myth: Kayotsarga is merely a physical austerity aimed at torturing or neglecting the body.
misconceptions.reality: Kayotsarga does involve disciplined stillness and the renunciation of physical comfort, but its purpose is not self-torture. Primary texts frame it as a practice of repentance, purification, and contemplation of the soul’s true nature. The body is respected as a vehicle, yet consciously de-centered so that attachment to it loosens. The "giving up" in kayotsarga refers to relinquishing clinging and ego-identification, not harming or despising the body.

misconceptions.myth: Kayotsarga is relevant only for monks and nuns and has no place in lay Jain practice.
misconceptions.reality: While kayotsarga is one of the six essentials of ascetic life and is practiced intensively by monks and nuns, laypeople also engage in kayotsarga within daily rites such as sāmāyika and pratikramaṇa. The concept of kāyotsargapratimā in graded lay stages shows that forms of kayotsarga—adapted to lay responsibilities—are recognized as important steps in spiritual progress. The intensity and duration may differ, but the core discipline of detachment and repentance is shared.

misconceptions.myth: Kayotsarga alone guarantees immediate liberation, regardless of ethical conduct or other spiritual disciplines.
misconceptions.reality: Narratives about tirthankaras and Bahubali attaining liberation in kayotsarga highlight its importance, but canonical doctrine insists that liberation arises from the complete path of right faith, right knowledge, and right conduct, supported by vows, restraints, and meditative practices. Kayotsarga is one powerful component of this path, especially for karmic shedding and equanimity, yet it must be integrated with ethical living, non-violence, and other observances to lead toward moksha.
